title: Senator says NT doesn't 'want to stick to' terms of $4b housing deal

By Emma Masters

Topic:Housing Policy

Two levels of government are in a deadlock over the NT Remote Housing agreement, which was designed to build more homes for Indigenous communities, town camps and homelands. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

Federal parliament has heard the Commonwealth and Northern Territory governments are deadlocked on the NT Remote Housing plan.

The jointly funded deal promised to build 2,700 new homes in 10 years.

Indigenous Australians Minister Malarndirri McCarthy says the NT will get its funding when it meets the criteria.

The federal and Northern Territory governments are in a deadlock over a multi-billion-dollar project to build thousands of new homes in remote Aboriginal communities, with concerns the project could deliver fewer than half the number originally planned.

Jointly funded in 2024, the NT Remote Housing agreement is aimed at reducing overcrowding and improving housing quality in the Territory's Indigenous communities, town camps and homelands.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has announced the 10-year agreement, which is expected to see up to 270 homes built each year, during a visit to the Northern Territory.

The $4 billion project promised to deliver 2,700 new homes over 10 years, but the NT government has recently asked to renegotiate the agreement.

In federal parliament on Wednesday, Senator Lidia Thorpe tabled documents she said showed $330 million in Commonwealth funding due under the agreement "has not been delivered and the Northern Territory government has provided no progress reports".

"Building is behind schedule, construction targets are being reduced, reporting is missing, funding isn't flowing, and mob are telling you that NT is not working for them," she said.

On Wednesday, Lidia Thorpe tabled documents and shared her concerns over the housing plan for the remote NT. (AAP: Mick Tsikas)

Federal Indigenous Australians minister and senator for the NT, Malarndirri McCarthy, said when the NT government "meets certain criteria, then [it] will receive the funding".

Senator McCarthy told parliament the NT's Country Liberal Party (CLP) government wanted more money from the agreement and that it "wants to reduce the number of homes down to 1,800 or maybe 1,100".

"They want to remove a certain amount of money from it for administration and for the land, in terms of where the houses will be built, in terms of making sure the land is ready."

NT Housing Minister Steve Edgington was contacted for comment but did not respond by deadline.

Late last month, Mr Edgington told ABC Radio Alice Springs that 400 houses had so far been built under the agreement, but that he could not detail how much had been spent to build them.

Steve Edgington has previously said the NT government faces a variety of pressures that impact on its ability to deliver on the agreement. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

He argued more money was needed to cover additional costs because "what we're facing at the moment is a whole range of different pressures on the program".

"We've seen significant increases in cost due to the global fuel crisis — around construction, freight, fuel, labour, infrastructure — and all those servicing costs have increased substantially, not just over the last 12 months, but in the last six months," he said at the time.

"Some of the costs are anywhere between $300,000 and around about $600,000, just to bring a block on to have that ready to build a house on.

"So these costs, which include the headworks, the power, water, sewage, all of those things which are essential components to build a home, are escalating out bush at the moment."

Senator Thorpe told the ABC she backed the federal government in rejecting the NT government's proposal to redistribute funds from the agreement for administration and headworks.

She called for Senator McCarthy to dump the NT government from managing the project and to instead directly fund Aboriginal organisations to do the work.

Lidia Thorpe wants the government to directly fund Aboriginal organisations to do the work in remote communities. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"The Northern Territory government need to basically move over and the minister needs to step in and bypass, which she has the power to do, and fund these organisations directly," she said.

The documents tabled by Senator Thorpe also included a joint statement from the Aboriginal members of the agreement's Joint Steering Committee, dated September 2025.

Many Aboriginal people in Tennant Creek live in overcrowded makeshift shelters with no running water or electricity as they wait up to a decade for a home. But experts say the social housing being built is not safe for today's climate, let alone the future.

In it, the members said they held "some serious concerns about the approach of the [NT government], in particular the Department of Housing", and called for the Indigenous Australians minister to "intervene where [the CLP] are falling short and hold them accountable".

The members' concerns included a "lack of clear reporting from the department and a reluctance to share data", along with "repeated comments by the department around the lack of capacity to do anything more than business as usual" on improving repairs and maintenance in the remote NT.

The statement said the Aboriginal committee members had "diminishing confidence that the department has a long-term strategic vision or has the capacity and willingness to change the way they currently do business".

The ABC understands the Joint Steering Committee — which is comprised of representatives from both governments, Aboriginal Housing NT and the four NT land councils — is due to meet next week.
